items.title: FreeRDP from 3.29.0 before 3.32.0 contains an integer overflow in the Apple audin backends ...
items.summary: FreeRDP from 3.29.0 before 3.32.0 contains an integer overflow in the Apple audin backends (audin_mac.m, audin_ios.m), which compute the audio queue buffer size as FramesPerPacket * 2 * nChannels in UINT32 arithmetic, bypassing the CVE-2026-91962 fix. A malicious RDP server can send FramesPerPacket of 2^30 in the audin Open PDU to wrap the multiplication, causing undersized AudioQueueAllocateBuffer allocations and a heap out-of-bounds write in macOS and iOS clients.

items.title: The Popup Box plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary Shortcode Execution in versions 6.4...
items.summary: The Popup Box plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary Shortcode Execution in versions 6.4.1 to 6.4.2. This is due to the ays_popup_get_user_ip() function reading the client-controlled Client-IP / X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded / X-Forwarded / Forwarded-For request headers, sanitizing them only with sanitize_text_field() (which does not strip the bracket, quote, space, or '=' characters used by shortcode syntax), substituting the value into a popup body wherever the %%user_ip_address%% token appears (a raw str_replace with no escaping in Ays_Pb_Data::replace_message_variables()), and then passing the resulting body to do_shortcode() in Ays_Pb_Public::ays_autoembed() at output on the wp_footer hook. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary registered shortcodes with attacker-supplied attributes on the server whenever an administrator has added the %%user_ip_address%% token to a popup's Custom Content body, which can be leveraged to read arbitrary data or perform other actions exposed by shortcodes installed on the site.

items.title: The Apache Airflow SSH provider hook disables SSH host-key verification by default: unless ...
items.summary:
The Apache Airflow SSH provider hook disables SSH host-key verification by default: unless `host_key` is configured or `no_host_key_check` is explicitly set to false, it accepts any server key. This affects SSH and SFTP connections that rely on the default. An attacker in a machine-in-the-middle position between the worker and the SSH or SFTP server can impersonate the server and capture the credentials or data a task sends.

Users of apache-airflow-providers-ssh and apache-airflow-providers-sftp are recommended to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-ssh 7.0.0 and apache-airflow-providers-sftp 7.0.0 or later. The deferrable SFTP code paths had the same default and are covered separately by CVE-2026-94135; apache-airflow-providers-sftp 7.0.0 fixes both.

items.title: The Apache Airflow Keycloak provider's multi-team provisioning (`_attach_team_permissions`)...
items.summary:
The Apache Airflow Keycloak provider's multi-team provisioning (`_attach_team_permissions`) granted every team role global read access to audit logs. Deployments that enable multi-team mode with the Keycloak auth manager and provision teams through it are affected: any authenticated member of one team could read other teams' audit events through the UI or the event-log API.

Users of apache-airflow-providers-keycloak are recommended to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-keycloak 0.11.1 or later.

items.title: The Apache Airflow SFTP provider's deferrable code paths (`SFTPTrigger`, `SFTPHookAsync`, ...
items.summary:
The Apache Airflow SFTP provider's deferrable code paths (`SFTPTrigger`, `SFTPHookAsync`, `SFTPClientPool`) disable SSH host-key verification by default unless the connection explicitly sets `no_host_key_check` to false. Deployments that run SFTP sensors or operators in deferrable mode are affected. An attacker in a machine-in-the-middle position between the triggerer and the SFTP server can impersonate the server and capture the credentials or data exchanged.

Users of apache-airflow-providers-sftp are recommended to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-sftp 7.0.0 or later. This is a separate defect from CVE-2026-94134 (the synchronous SSH hook default, which also affects the SFTP hook); users who applied the fix for one also need this release for the other - apache-airflow-providers-sftp 7.0.0 fixes both.

items.title: The Apache Airflow Keycloak auth manager did not end the session on logout: the logout route...
items.summary:
The Apache Airflow Keycloak auth manager did not end the session on logout: the logout route revoked the presented token, but `KeycloakJWTMiddleware` then issued a new, unrevoked token on the same response, so the user stayed logged in. Deployments using the Keycloak auth manager are affected: after a user logs out, anyone with later access to the same browser (for example on a shared workstation) can continue to act as that user.

Users of apache-airflow-providers-keycloak are recommended to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-keycloak 0.11.1 or later.

items.title: TanStack Router: Unauthenticated reflected XSS in TanStack Start server-function responses
items.summary:
## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can craft a URL to a server function in an affected TanStack Start app. If someone opens the link, the app can return attacker-controlled HTML from its own origin and run the attacker's JavaScript there. The script can access same-origin data available to that visitor and make requests with their authority.

## Cause

The server-function transport can pass request payload fields into internal middleware state instead of limiting them to public input fields. A malformed payload can leave an attacker-controlled result in the error path. Response handling can then treat a response-shaped object as an HTTP response.

## Affected versions

Published versions of `@tanstack/start-server-core`, `@tanstack/react-start`, `@tanstack/solid-start`, and `@tanstack/vue-start` from `1.143.12` up to, but not including, their respective patched versions are affected. The patched versions are `@tanstack/start-server-core@1.169.39`, `@tanstack/react-start@1.168.60`, `@tanstack/solid-start@1.168.57`, and `@tanstack/vue-start@1.168.56`.

## Fix

The fix limits client-supplied server-function input to public fields and validates responses at the server boundary. Upgrade to the corresponding patched package version.

## Temporary mitigations

For the configured server-function path, usually `/_serverFn/*`, an edge or WAF rule can consider blocking requests without the literal `x-tsr-serverFn: true` header and browser document navigations such as `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` or `Accept: text/html`. A restrictive Content Security Policy on server-function responses can provide another browser-side restriction. These are mitigation suggestions, not a complete fix. The header is client-controlled and is not authentication. Test rules against legitimate GET and POST server functions and use a matching version-specific backport where possible.

## Credits

Lovable helped us discover and report this issue. We thank them for their help.

items.title: Pipecat: Public exposure of Pipecat’s development runner can allow unauthenticated bot session creation
items.summary:
Pipecat’s built-in development runner exposes endpoints that create bot sessions and, for the Daily transport, paid Daily rooms. These development endpoints intentionally do not authenticate callers.

The runner binds to localhost by default and is designed exclusively for local development. It is not built or supported as a production server. Exploitation therefore requires an operator to deliberately make the development runner reachable from an untrusted network, such as by setting --host 0.0.0.0, publishing its port, or using a public tunnel without access controls.

If exposed in this way, an unauthenticated caller may invoke endpoints including /start, /daily, and /daily-dialin-webhook. Depending on the endpoint and configuration, this can create a bot session or Daily room and may return a room URL and join token. Repeated requests may also consume local resources and third-party service quotas.

The consequences of interacting with a launched bot depend on that bot’s configuration and connected tools. Access to external systems or sensitive information is not an inherent capability of the development runner and is therefore not included as a general impact.

Pipecat 1.6.0 clarifies this security boundary in two ways:

- The development runner displays a prominent startup banner identifying it as a development tool.
- The documentation explicitly states that the runner must not be used as a production server or exposed directly to untrusted traffic.

The local development documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-locally) identifies the unauthenticated endpoints, lack of rate limiting, and risks of public exposure. The production deployment documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-in-production) directs users to a production dispatcher or managed runtime and describes minimum protections for limited prototype use.

### Resolution

> Pipecat 1.6.0 documents and surfaces the intended security boundary of the development runner. The unauthenticated development behavior remains by design. Users must not
> expose the runner directly to untrusted networks; production deployments require an authenticated dispatcher or managed runtime.

items.title: Podman: The `podman run` command can be instructed to disable almost all sandboxing by image annotation
items.summary:
### Impact
Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the `podman container checkpoint` command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the `podman run` command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When `podman run` detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, `podman run --cap-drop=ALL` on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore `--cap-drop=all` and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name`. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in `podman run` allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

### Patch
The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main)
ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1)
7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

### Workarounds
Images being pulled should be scanned for the `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name` annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

### Credits
This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

items.title: JupyterLab: Command link trust prompt in JupyterLab can trust a document other than the one clicked
items.summary:
## Description

A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.

Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: `markdownviewer:trust` uses `tracker.currentWidget`, and `notebook:trust` uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.

Users are affected if all of the following are true:

- they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;
- they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;
- they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and
- a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file

### Impact

The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in [GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg).

The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.

#### Notebooks are written to disk

When the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. `notebook:trust` marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted.

A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk.

### Patches

JupyterLab [`v4.6.4`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.6.4) and [`v4.5.11`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.5.11) contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked.

Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update `jupyterlab` package too.

### Workarounds

Given the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below. 

Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether:

```json
{
  "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": {
    "allowCommandLinker": false
  }
}
```

In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones.

If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.

items.title: SFTPGo source-side file-pattern filter bypass during copy operations
items.summary:
### Summary

File pattern filters (`denied_patterns` / `allowed_patterns`) were evaluated on the destination of a copy only. A user holding the copy permission could copy a file denied by the filters to a permitted name and then read it. A recursive directory copy reproduced the contents of a restricted directory under a path where the filters do not deny them, and the hide policy was affected in the same way: a file reported as missing by stat and by directory listings could still be copied.

### Details

An authenticated user can read the contents of files that the file pattern filters are configured to deny them. Nothing else is bypassed: the home directory, the virtual folder layout and the per-directory permissions are all still enforced, and both ends of the copy are paths the account can already reach. No access to other accounts and no administrative capability.

items.title: Claude Code: Plugin Hash Pin Bypass Allows Bypass of Hash Pinning
items.summary:
The plugin install flow in Claude Code and Claude Desktop checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA using `git checkout` without verifying that the resulting HEAD matched the pinned SHA. An attacker controlling a plugin's upstream repository could create a branch named identically to the pinned 40-character SHA, causing the checkout to silently resolve to the attacker's branch tip instead of the reviewed commit, resulting in attacker-controlled code being installed bypassing the pinned hash. Exploitation required a user to install a malicious plugin, pin to a safe hash, and for the plugin source to be hosted on a git host that permitted SHA-shaped branch names.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix already. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Thank you to Or Nevo Michrowski of Air Security for reporting this issue.

items.title: containerd: Unpack DoS via repeated opaque whiteouts
items.summary:
### Impact

A vulnerability exists in containerd's layer unpack handler where the processing of certain image layers causes superlinear time complexity. During the unpack operation, specific file configurations within the layer can trigger repeated directory traversals.

Consequently, pulling or importing a maliciously crafted image can result in increased unpack times and a moderate increase in CPU usage. This delays container startup, even if the compressed image layers are small. Additionally, in orchestrators like Kubernetes that apply concurrency limits to image pulls, these excessively long operations can reduce the available concurrency for other pulls, potentially delaying unrelated container deployments.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.5, 2.2.8, 2.0.12, and 1.7.35. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue. Users are advised to only pull and import trusted images from known registries until the patch can be applied.

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank Jakub Ciolek of AlphaSense for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

items.title: Distribution: Client `manifests.Get()` does not verify returned content against requested digest
items.summary:
### Summary

`registry/client.(*manifests).Get(ctx, dgst, …)` fetches a manifest by digest but never hashes the returned body and compares it against the requested digest. A malicious or compromised registry, or any MITM on the registry connection, can serve arbitrary manifest bytes in response to a digest-pinned request and the client returns the substituted content transparently to the caller. Any application relying on digest pinning for supply-chain integrity — image policy controllers, mirrors, pull-through caches — is silently undermined. The bundled pull-through proxy (`registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go`) is itself an unguarded consumer and is directly exploitable.

### Details

**Root cause:** `registry/client/repository.go:488-505` reads the response body and passes it directly to `distribution.UnmarshalManifest` without ever computing `digest.FromBytes(body)` and comparing against the caller-supplied `dgst`. The `Docker-Content-Digest` response header is parsed (lines 251-292 in `descriptorFromResponse`) only to populate an out-parameter (`ReturnContentDigest`) and is itself server-supplied — it is never recomputed from the body, so a lying server can set it to whatever value the caller requested while delivering different bytes.

**Attack path:** An attacker who controls the registry endpoint (malicious registry, compromised upstream, DNS hijack, or TLS MITM) responds to `GET /v2/{name}/manifests/{digest}` with:
1. `Docker-Content-Digest: <requested-digest>` (forged header)
2. A body containing a different, attacker-chosen manifest

The client calls `distribution.UnmarshalManifest` on the substituted body, returns the attacker's manifest as if it were the pinned content, and the caller has no way to detect the substitution.

**Why it matters:** The entire value of digest pinning is to guarantee content-addressable integrity against exactly this threat model (hostile or MITM server). The `registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go:42-87` pull-through cache calls `remoteManifests.Get(ctx, dgst)` and immediately writes the result to local storage with no re-verification — so a poisoned remote can permanently inject a bad manifest into the mirror cache, affecting all subsequent consumers.

Relevant code path (`repository.go`, simplified):
```go
// line ~496
func (ms *manifests) Get(ctx context.Context, dgst digest.Digest, options ...distribution.ManifestServiceOption) (distribution.Manifest, error) {
    ...
    resp, err := ms.client.Get(u)
    ...
    body, err := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)  // no size limit, no digest check
    ...
    m, _, err := distribution.UnmarshalManifest(ct, body)  // returns attacker bytes
    return m, err
}
```

### PoC

**go.mod:**
```
module poc

go 1.24.10

require (
        github.com/distribution/reference v0.6.0
        github.com/docker/distribution v2.8.3+incompatible
        github.com/opencontainers/go-digest v1.0.0
)

require (
        github.com/beorn7/perks v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/go-metrics v0.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/libtrust v0.0.0-20160708172513-aabc10ec26b7 // indirect
        github.com/golang/protobuf v1.3.2 // indirect
        github.com/gorilla/mux v1.8.1 // indirect
        github.com/matttproud/golang_protobuf_extensions v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/opencontainers/image-spec v1.1.1 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_golang v1.1.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_model v0.0.0-20190129233127-fd36f4220a90 // indirect

        github.com/prometheus/procfs v0.0.3 // indirect

items.title: Qwik: Crashing any Qwik Server via Resource thenable
items.summary:
### Summary

A Qwik server in the default configuration can be crashed with one unauthenticated HTTP request. During qwik-json body parsing, `ResourceSerializer.$fill$` does `Promise.resolve(resource._resolved)`. If `_resolved` is a plain object whose `.then` is a QRL for an unregistered symbol, the async QRL rejects, the rejection is orphaned, and Node terminates the process via its default unhandled-rejection policy.

### Impact

One unauthenticated request crashes the server. Looping keeps every replica dead as long as the attacker sends requests.

items.title: containerd CRI plugin: Checkpoint restore bypasses destination security context
items.summary:
### Impact

A vulnerability in containerd's CRI implementation allows a container restored from an untrusted checkpoint via the `CreateContainer` API to bypass the destination security context and execute with elevated privileges. When restoring a container from a checkpoint archive or annotated OCI image, CRIU restores process credentials, Linux capabilities, `no_new_privs`, and seccomp state directly from checkpoint data rather than enforcing the destination CRI `ContainerConfig`. An attacker who can run a container with a crafted checkpoint image can execute processes as root with full capabilities and no enforced seccomp filters despite restrictive security policies requested by the orchestrator. Additionally, containerd's CRI status reporting reflects the requested configuration rather than the actual restored process state, masking the privilege discrepancy from orchestrators. This issue affects Linux systems running containerd with CRI checkpoint restore enabled; users not utilizing CRI checkpoint restore are not affected.

### Patches

This bug has been addressed in containerd 2.2.7 and 2.3.4 by disabling checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer` by default.  The feature has been removed entirely in containerd 2.4.0. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue. Running containers that were restored from untrusted checkpoints should be stopped, deleted, and recreated.

Users who rely on restore via the `CreateContainer` API can re-enable the feature by setting the new `enable_experimental_restore_via_create` configuration option. However, enabling restore via `CreateContainer` leaves this vulnerability present, as containerd cannot enforce destination security policy during CRIU process restoration. 

### Workarounds

On unpatched versions, containerd does not provide a configuration option to disable checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer`. Deployments should restrict container creation permissions to trusted users, validate container image registries, or use admission controllers to reject images containing checkpoint data.

### References

* [CRIU image security](https://checkpoint-restore.github.io/criu/security/image-security.html)

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank @l2yyd5 and @berkpolatCE for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

* Open an issue in [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/new/choose)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

To report a security issue in containerd:

items.title: kin-openapi: Incomplete Fix for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5: Three Unpatched nil-Items Panic Paths in openapi3filter
items.summary:
## Summary

The fix for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 addressed a nil-pointer dereference that occurs when an OpenAPI 3.1 array schema omits the `items` keyword (which is legal under JSON Schema 2020-12). That fix patched three decoder paths: the standalone `parseArray` function, the top-level array check in `UrlencodedBodyDecoder`, and `MultipartBodyDecoder`.

Three additional crash paths were missed. All of them reach the unguarded `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` method (`openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:576`) or the unguarded array branch in `buildResObj` (line 1015):

1. **Query parameters** with `type: array` and no `items`.
2. **deepObject** query parameters containing an array property with no `items`.
3. **URL-encoded request bodies** where the array lives inside an `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` sub-schema. This path bypasses the guard added by the GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 fix, because that guard only inspects top-level properties.

Each path is triggerable by an unauthenticated client and produces a deterministic nil-pointer panic during request validation.

## Details
### Root Cause

The three paths patched for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 each received a nil-`items` guard:

```go
// standalone parseArray (line 1143) -- GUARDED
func parseArray(raw []string, schemaRef *openapi3.SchemaRef) ([]any, error) {
	if schemaRef.Value.Items == nil || schemaRef.Value.Items.Value == nil { ... }

// UrlencodedBodyDecoder top-level property loop (line 1441) -- GUARDED
if propSchema.Value.Items == nil || propSchema.Value.Items.Value == nil { ... }

// MultipartBodyDecoder (line 1587) -- GUARDED
if valueSchema.Value.Items == nil { ... }
```

But `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` (line 576), which handles query-parameter and urlencoded-body array decoding, has **no** such guard:

```go
func (d *urlValuesDecoder) parseArray(raw []string, schemaRef *openapi3.SchemaRef) ([]any, error) {
	var value []any
	for i, v := range raw {
		item, err := d.parseValue(v, schemaRef.Value.Items) // Items is nil -> panic in parseValue
```

`parseValue` immediately dereferences the schema it is handed:

```go
func (d *urlValuesDecoder) parseValue(v string, schema *openapi3.SchemaRef) (any, error) {
	if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {   // schema == nil here -> nil pointer dereference
```

For the deepObject path, `buildResObj` (line 1015) has the same gap. Its array branch recurses with `schema.Value.Items` (line 1028), which can be nil, and the recursive call dereferences it at line 1015:

```go
case schema.Value.Type.Is("array"):
	// ...
	for i := range arr {
		r, err := buildResObj(params, mapKeys, strconv.Itoa(i), schema.Value.Items) // nil Items
```

For the allOf body path, `UrlencodedBodyDecoder` validates only top-level `schema.Value.Properties` (line 1429-1449). But `decodeSchemaConstructs` (line 1474) recursively walks `AllOf` / `AnyOf` / `OneOf` sub-schemas and calls `decodeProperty` on their properties, which never pass through the top-level guard and reach `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray`.

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (cloned at tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- Go 1.26.7
- Each PoC calls `doc.Validate()` first to prove the spec is legal, then drives `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest` directly

### Path 1: Query parameter array without items

Spec (query param `ids` is `type: array`, no `items`), request `GET /test?ids=1&ids=2`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec (type: array with no items is legal under OAS 3.1)
Calling ValidateRequest directly (no net/http recover)...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal 0xc0000005 code=0x0 addr=0x20 ...]
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseValue(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:605
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:580
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).DecodeArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:569

## Summary

kin-openapi's spec loader and spec-time validator both handle circular schema references safely: the loader resolves circular `$ref`s on purpose (to support recursive data structures), and `Schema.validate()` uses stack-based cycle detection. `Validate()` therefore accepts a schema whose `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` chain refers back to itself, returning no error.

The runtime validators do not have that protection. When such a schema is used for request or response validation, the recursion through the combinator chain is unbounded. In Go this produces a **fatal stack overflow** (`runtime: goroutine stack exceeds ... limit` / `fatal error: stack overflow`), which is **not** a recoverable panic. `recover()` cannot catch it, so `net/http`'s per-connection recovery does not help. The entire process is terminated, including all goroutines serving unrelated clients.

Two independent unguarded recursion sites were confirmed:

1. `openapi3/schema.go` — `visitJSON` / `visitXOFOperations` (reached by `VisitJSON`, i.e. response validation and direct schema validation).
2. `openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go` — `decodeValue` (reached first during request parameter decoding). The report also identifies the same gap in `urlValuesDecoder.parseValue` and `buildResObj`/`buildFromSchemas`.

## Details 
### Root Cause

`Schema.validate()` has cycle detection (`openapi3/schema.go:1396`):

```go
func (schema *Schema) validate(ctx context.Context, stack []*Schema) ([]*Schema, error) {
	if slices.Contains(stack, schema) {
		return stack, nil
	}
	// ...
	stack = append(stack, schema)
```

The runtime visitor has none. `visitJSON` (line 1951) calls `visitXOFOperations` (line 2189), which iterates the combinator slice and calls `visitJSON` again on each sub-schema:

	// ...
	for idx, item := range v { // v = schema.OneOf / AnyOf / AllOf
		v := item.Value
		// no check for item.Value == schema (or any ancestor)
		if err := v.visitJSON(settings, tempValue); err != nil { // recurses forever on a cycle
```

The request-decoding path has the same structure in `decodeValue` (`openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:270`):

```go
func decodeValue(dec valueDecoder, param string, sm *openapi3.SerializationMethod, schema *openapi3.SchemaRef, required bool) (any, bool, error) {
	if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
		for _, sr := range schema.Value.AllOf {
			value, f, err = decodeValue(dec, param, sm, sr, required) // no cycle check
```

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- Go 1.26.7

### Path A: response / direct schema validation (`VisitJSON`)

	Type:       &openapi3.Types{"object"},
	Properties: openapi3.Schemas{"name": {Value: &openapi3.Schema{Type: &openapi3.Types{"string"}}}},
}
recursiveSchema.AllOf = openapi3.SchemaRefs{{Value: recursiveSchema}} // circular

_ = recursiveSchema.Validate(ctx)                       // accepted, no error
_ = recursiveSchema.VisitJSON(map[string]any{"name": "test"}) // crashes

items.title: kin-openapi: YAML NaN/Inf Values Bypass Built-in Guards and Panic via OAS 3.1 Validation Path
items.summary:
## Summary

kin-openapi guards against `NaN` and `Inf` values in its built-in schema visitor (`visitJSON`) by returning `ErrSchemaInputNaN` / `ErrSchemaInputInf` when a `float64` input violates those constraints. For OAS 3.1 specs, however, `Schema.VisitJSON` routes through `useJSONSchema2020`, which hands the value directly to `santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` v6.0.2 without applying the same guard.

Inside `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.2, `numValidate` builds a `*big.Rat` from the input via `big.Rat.SetString(fmt.Sprintf("%v", v))`. For `NaN`/`Inf` this parse fails silently and returns `nil`. `numValidate` then dereferences the nil `*big.Rat` (in `math/big.(*Rat).Cmp`), producing a Go runtime panic.

An attacker delivers this by sending an HTTP request with `Content-Type: application/yaml` (or `application/x-yaml`) and a YAML body containing `.nan`, `.inf`, or `-.inf`. The `YamlBodyDecoder` decodes those tokens into `math.NaN()` / `math.Inf(±1)` (standard YAML 1.2 behavior), and they propagate to the unguarded `useJSONSchema2020` path whenever the schema declares a numeric constraint (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, or `multipleOf`).

## Details
### Root Cause

The built-in visitor `visitJSON` at `openapi3/schema.go:1968` guards NaN/Inf explicitly:

```go
case float64:
    if math.IsNaN(value) {
        return ErrSchemaInputNaN
    }
    if math.IsInf(value, 0) {
        return ErrSchemaInputInf
    }
```

For OAS 3.1 specs, `VisitJSON` dispatches to `useJSONSchema2020` (`openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:204`), which contains no such guard:

```go
func (schema *Schema) useJSONSchema2020(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) error {
    validator, err := newJSONSchemaValidator(schema)
    if err != nil {
        return schema.visitJSON(settings, value)
    }
    return validator.validate(value)      // value handed straight through
}
```

`jsonSchemaValidator.validate` calls `jsonschema/v6.Schema.Validate` (line 146), which reaches `numValidate` in v6.0.2. There, `big.Rat.SetString(fmt.Sprintf("%v", v))` returns `(nil, false)` for `NaN`/`Inf`, and the code dereferences the `nil` `*big.Rat` in `Rat.Cmp`, causing the panic.

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 v6.0.2 (transitive dep)
- Go 1.26.7

### Spec

Minimal OAS 3.1 spec (`spec.yaml`) declaring a YAML body with a numeric constraint:

```yaml
openapi: '3.1.0'
info: { title: Test, version: '1.0' }
paths:
  /test:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/yaml:
            schema:
              type: number
              minimum: 0
      responses:
        '200': { description: OK }
```

### Trigger

A single `POST /test` with `Content-Type: application/yaml` and body `.nan`, `.inf`, or `-.inf`. All three variants panic:

```
=== RUN   TestNaNInf
[nan]    PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[inf]    PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[neginf] PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
```

    C:/Program Files/Go/src/math/big/rat.go:492

items.title: Talos Linux: Support bundle does not redact registry credentials
items.summary:
### Summary
When generating a support bundle with `talosctl support` the credentials entered for private registries are included in the bundle.


### Details

Within the generated support bundle, inside `resources/registryconfigs.cri.talos.dev.yaml` the `auth` field of the spec is retained.
The same, potentially sensitive information is present within `etcfilespecs.files.talos.dev.yaml`.

### PoC

Simply run `talosctl -n [...] support` on a cluster with a `RegistryAuthConfig` resource 

### Impact

The problem itself is minor, however, anyone who has ever uploaded a support.zip bundle on a github issue, slack thread or public forum could have potentially leaked their internal authentication parameters for a private registry.

In most situations, if the network and credentials are set correctly, this should not be a problem. On the other hand, if the affected registry is publicly accessible, and the provided credentials have write access to it, this could lead to possibly serious consequences, from denial of service, to data loss and possibly existing tag hijacking leading to supply chain compromise, for the affected parties which were under the impression that the support bundle is redacted of sensitive information and thus can be shared publicly.


### Notes

Talos 1.14+ by default encrypts the support bundle to the age recipients specified (defaulting to siderolabs GitHub org members), so the impact is even lower.

### Environment

- Talos version: v1.13.0
- Kubernetes version: 1.35.3
- Platform: amd64

items.title: KEDA: Privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin via KEDA TriggerAuthentication
items.summary:
## Summary

A namespace admin who creates a `TriggerAuthentication` and a `ScaledObject` in their own namespace can make the KEDA operator send its own ServiceAccount token to a tenant-controlled URL. That token holds `["*"]/["*"] get` cluster-wide, so it reads every Secret in every namespace, plus `batch/jobs` and `horizontalpodautoscalers` create/delete cluster-wide, `*/scale` update on any workload, `validatingwebhookconfigurations` update (rewrite or disable cluster admission), and `apiservices` update (hijack aggregated API routing). This is effectively privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin in real environments: a cluster-wide Secret read alone is enough to find a token for a more privileged ServiceAccount, and the cluster-wide `batch/jobs` create lets the attacker run a workload in any namespace whose Pod Security Admission level permits it (or that is PSA-exempt, such as `kube-system` , `kyverno`) to reach the node filesystem and a control-plane kubeconfig.

This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-68476: its content filter only requires the loaded file to be a JWT whose subject begins with `system:serviceaccount:`, which the operator's own projected token satisfies by construction. The destination field `hashiCorpVault.address` is unvalidated.

items.title: Argo CD: AppProject destination-namespace and resource restrictions bypassed by PreDelete/PostDelete resource hooks
items.summary:
### Impact

Argo CD checks an Application's AppProject before it creates resources during a sync. That check covers destination namespaces and servers, cluster-scoped resource allow and deny lists, and namespaced resource allow and deny lists, including resource names. PreDelete and PostDelete hooks skip it. When the Application is deleted, Argo CD creates those hooks with the application-controller's credentials on the destination cluster.

All versions from v2.10.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.9.22 and earlier are not. PostDelete hooks were introduced in [dcc17f70bf](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) (2023-12-18, [#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)) and first released in v2.10.0. That creation path has never applied the project check. PreDelete hooks, added in [3bf3d8a212](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) (2025-12-05, [#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)) and first released in v3.3.0, use the same path. v3.2.12 and earlier do not have PreDelete hooks. PreSync, Sync, PostSync, and SyncFail hooks still go through the project check.

A user who can push to the Git repository an Application syncs from can commit a hook whose namespace, group, kind, or name the AppProject would refuse on sync. The controller adds the delete finalizer when it sees the hook, and the Application stays Synced until someone deletes it. Deleting the Application creates the hook. What that can reach is bounded by the application-controller's access to the destination cluster. In a typical install that access is broad, so a tenant can create a cluster-scoped object such as a `ClusterRoleBinding`, or an object in a namespace the project does not allow. A hook with no deletion policy is removed after it succeeds. A deletion policy that does not remove the hook on success leaves the object in the cluster. A hook such as a Job can create further objects that Argo CD does not clean up.

### Patches

A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:

* v3.6.0-rc2
* v3.5.4
* v3.4.10
* v3.3.15

The fix applies the same AppProject destination and resource checks used on sync before creating a PreDelete or PostDelete hook.

Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration setting that applies the project check to delete hooks while those hooks stay in use.

* Do not grant untrusted users write access to Git repositories that back Applications in restrictive AppProjects.
* Limit who can delete Applications. Deletion is what runs PreDelete and PostDelete hooks.
* Tighten the application-controller's Kubernetes access so a hook cannot reach sensitive namespaces or APIs.

### Credits

The Argo CD team would like to thank @RealFakeAccount, @AdamKorcz, @0xshylines, @thevilledev, @HenriWilliams, @cherez0ff, @ARSB1, and @zwindler for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).

items.title: kin-openapi: ValidationHandler security-requirement bypass via encoded-path operation confusion
items.summary:
## Summary

`openapi3filter.ValidationHandler.Middleware` validates requests with kin-openapi's
legacy router, which selects an OpenAPI operation from the decoded `URL.Path`. The
method is documented as implementing `gorilla/mux.MiddlewareFunc`, but a downstream
gorilla/mux router configured with `UseEncodedPath()` selects its handler from the
encoded representation (`URL.RawPath`).

An unauthenticated request such as `/public%2Fstatus` can therefore be validated as an
intentionally public operation (`/public/status`) and then dispatched to a protected
operation (`/{id}`). The configured, rejecting `AuthenticationFunc` is never invoked,
and the protected downstream handler runs.

This is distinct from GHSA-r277-6w6q-xmqw. The behavior below uses an explicit
authentication callback that rejects missing credentials and remains reproducible
after the v0.144.0 fix for the unsafe default callback.

## Affected products

- Product: `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi`
- Component: `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler.Middleware`
- Confirmed post-GHSA affected releases: v0.144.0, v0.145.0, and v0.146.0
- Reporter attestation: each listed release was checked out separately, the attached
  single-file test was copied into `openapi3filter/`, and that test passed; maintainers
  should independently confirm the version range
- Confirmed affected development revision: `d33e44e67734dcde81b576582185e1343fb3985d`
- v0.143.0 also reproduces this mechanism, but GHSA-r277-6w6q-xmqw already provides a

items.summary:
### Summary

`openapi3filter` decodes `deepObject`-style query parameters by looping over **every** key in the request's query string. Inside that loop it recompiles a **loop-invariant** regular expression on every iteration. The pattern depends only on the spec-defined parameter name, not on the loop variable, so it is compiled `N` times for `N` query keys instead of once. Because the number of query keys is attacker-controlled and unbounded, a single request with many junk query keys forces a proportional number of `regexp.MustCompile` calls, consuming CPU. A handful of concurrent requests can saturate all cores — an uncontrolled-resource-consumption denial of service.

This is **not** ReDoS: the pattern is fixed (`^<param>\[`) and matches in linear time. The cost is the **repeated compilation** of an invariant regexp, once per attacker-supplied query key.

### Details

In `openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go`, the `deepObject` branch of `urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject` builds a per-parameter property map by iterating over all query keys:

```go
case "deepObject":
    propsFn = func(params url.Values) (map[string]string, error) {
        props := make(map[string]string)
        for key, values := range params {                                            // req_resp_decoder.go:689
            if !regexp.MustCompile(fmt.Sprintf(`^%s\[`, regexp.QuoteMeta(param))).MatchString(key) { // :690
                continue
            }
            matches := deepObjectBracketRE.FindAllStringSubmatch(key, -1)
            ...
        }
        ...
    }
```

The regexp built at `req_resp_decoder.go:690` depends only on `param` — the parameter name defined in the OpenAPI spec — which is **constant** for the whole loop. Yet `regexp.MustCompile(...)` is invoked inside the `for key, values := range params` loop at `req_resp_decoder.go:689`, so it is recompiled once for every key present in the query string.

Contrast this with the already-hoisted, package-level regexp used two lines below:

```go
var deepObjectBracketRE = regexp.MustCompile(`\[(.*?)\]`) // req_resp_decoder.go:41
```

`deepObjectBracketRE` is compiled exactly once at package init and reused. The per-parameter pattern at `:690` should be compiled the same way (once, outside the loop), but instead is rebuilt on every iteration.

`regexp.MustCompile` costs on the order of a few microseconds per call. The number of iterations equals the number of query keys `N`, which the client fully controls (a ~1 MB URL holds roughly 100k keys). For each `deepObject` parameter `M` defined on the matched route, the request performs `N × M` compilations. The work is CPU-bound, happens during request validation before any handler logic, and scales linearly with request size, so an attacker converts cheap request bytes into expensive server CPU.

Affected code path: `ValidateRequest` → `ValidateParameter` → `decodeStyledParameter` → `urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject` (the `deepObject` case). Any operation with at least one `in: query`, `style: deepObject` parameter is exploitable.

### PoC

The following self-contained test (package `openapi3filter_test`) defines a spec with a single `deepObject` query parameter, then validates two requests that differ only in the number of junk query keys. Decoding time grows with the key count even though none of the junk keys are part of the parameter.

items.summary: ### Summary Dgraph `v25.3.8` exposes a Zero HTTP administrative surface that is unauthenticated when port `6080` is reachable. The exposed routes include: - `/state` - `/assign` - `/removeNode` - `/moveTablet` An unauthenticated request to `/removeNode?id=1&group=0` on a single-node standalone deployment breaks the Zero control plane and leaves Alpha repeatedly failing to reconnect to `localhost:5080`. ### Details The issue exists because Zero administrative HTTP endpoints are registered directly without any authentication or IP-whitelist wrapper. Relevant code paths: - `worker/server_state.go:41` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/run.go:295-301` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/http.go:106-129` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/zero.go:475-477` The relevant behavior is: - `disable-admin-http=false` by default - `/removeNode` accepts attacker-controlled `id` and `group` - `removeNode` forwards those directly into `Server.RemoveNode` - for `group=0`, `Server.RemoveNode` immediately calls `ProposePeerRemoval` This means a remote unauthenticated caller can directly trigger destructive membership operations if `6080` is exposed. ### PoC ### Read state without authentication ```bash curl -i http://127.0.0.1:6080/state ``` Observed response included: - Zero node `id=1` - `groupId=0` - `leader=true` - cluster topology and tablet state ### Write-capable route without authentication ```bash curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:6080/assign?what=nsids&num=1' ``` Observed response: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... {"startId":"1", "endId":"1", "readOnly":"0"} ``` This confirms the admin plane is not merely informational. ### Destructive unauthenticated removeNode ```bash curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:6080/removeNode?id=1&group=0' ``` Observed result: ```text curl: (52) Empty reply from server ``` Immediately afterward: ```bash curl -i http://127.0.0.1:6080/health ``` Observed result: ```text curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer ``` Alpha health was still locally reachable, but Alpha logs began repeatedly reporting: ```text dial tcp [::1]:5080: connect: connection refused ``` This confirms the request reached the destructive path and disrupted the Zero control plane. ### Impact Any deployment that exposes Zero HTTP on `6080` exposes destructive unauthenticated administrative capabilities. An attacker can: - read cluster topology and control-plane metadata - allocate IDs and timestamps - invoke destructive membership actions - disrupt the Zero control plane - indirectly destabilize Alpha nodes that depend on Zero connectivity This is a high-value unauthenticated administrative exposure and, in the reproduced case, a practical denial of service against the control plane.

items.title: tinytag: Infinite loop when parsing certain M4A files containing invalid atoms
items.summary:
### Impact
An M4A file containing a sub-atom with a size of zero in the `----` atom makes the parser enter an infinite loop, resulting in a denial-of-service for programs reading such files with tinytag.

### Patches
The issue has been fixed in tinytag 2.3.0, by reusing the primary atom parsing code path that contains appropriate size checks.

### Workarounds
No workarounds exist. Users must upgrade to tinytag 2.3.0.

items.title: copyparty FTP: upload outside defined volumes (limited path traversal)
items.summary:
The FTP and FTPS server -- if enabled -- would allow uploading to any folder that the copyparty process had permission to write to.

The FTP-server is default-disabled, and must be explicitly enabled in the config with global-option `ftp` or `ftps` to be affected. Additionally, SFTP was not affected at all; only FTP and FTPS.

This was not a full read/write path-traversal; it had the following limitations:
* Only applied to uploads; it was not possible to read/download existing files in this manner.
* The output filename was not fully controllable; a randomized suffix would always be appended to the filename.
* Existing files could not be overwritten or appended to; only new files could be created.
* Filesystem-permissions would prevent writing to system folders, as copyparty surely does not run as root in most deployments.
* Copyparty itself will not execute arbitrary files as code by default, so this vulnerability could not be used to execute arbitrary code through copyparty.

The main concern is the potential effect on other unrelated software which is running on the same system.

The severity is assuming the worst case (SC:H/SI:H), that the same machine is running some unrelated software that will execute new arbitrarily-named files as code, and that the copyparty process has sufficient privileges to write files into the config-folder of that unrelated software.

`fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` — **without HTML escaping**. The response is served
as `text/html; charset=utf-8`, and Vitess's default `acl` policy is
**allow-all**, so the endpoint is reachable by anyone who can hit the
vttablet's HTTP port (default `15999`, multiplexed with gRPC and MySQL
wire-protocol ports).

executes in the operator's browser with same-origin access to the

`/querylogz` (recent queries with bound values), `/txlogz` (transactions),
`/debug/env` (environment variables — may include MySQL/topology
credentials), `/debug/vars` (expvar stats), and `/debug/pprof/*` if

Untrusted local .mise.toml [settings] can set the shell interpreter args (unix/windows default_inline / default_file shell_args), yielding arbitrary command execution, because those command-interpreter settings were not added to the global_only denylist the CVE-2026-55448 fix relies on. items.title: kin-openapi spec loader panics on a self-referential additionalProperties $ref (nil-pointer DoS)
items.summary:
The defect
----------
Confirmed at HEAD (f0407d5, v0.144.0). openapi3/loader.go, inside resolveComponent's drill closure (around line 455), the case *SchemaRef branch for pathPart == "additionalProperties" dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value:

    case *SchemaRef:
        if pathPart == "additionalProperties" {
            if ap := c.Value.AdditionalProperties.Has; ap != nil {   // c.Value can be nil here
                cursor = *ap
            } else {
                cursor = c.Value.AdditionalProperties.Schema
            }
            attempted = true
        }

When a $ref fragment drills through .../additionalProperties of a schema whose Value is still nil (a pure, not-yet-resolved $ref, or a self-reference resolved before its own Value is set), c.Value is nil and the .AdditionalProperties access panics.

Input and attacker
-------------------
A tiny crafted OpenAPI document, one schema, no external refs, no network:

    openapi: 3.0.3
    info: {title: t, version: "1.0.0"}
    paths: {}
    components:
      schemas:
        A:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/A/additionalProperties'

Attacker model: any service or tool that loads an untrusted spec via the default openapi3.Loader (LoadFromData / LoadFromFile / LoadFromURI), e.g. a spec registry, an API-management platform ingesting user specs, a linter, or a converter. It crashes during LOAD (ResolveRefsIn), before Validate.

Verification level
------------------
EXECUTED with negative controls (agent-run go test at HEAD f0407d5, including yesterday's security merge; the bug is still present). The full stack pins LoadFromData:196 -> ResolveRefsIn:274 -> resolveSchemaRef:1048 -> resolveComponent:485 -> drill:439 -> :455, propagating to main(); no recover() in loader.go/schema.go (grep + trace). Two negative controls stay clean: drilling additionalProperties of a resolved schema loads fine (the existing TestIssue376 happy path), and a normal recursive schema loads fine, so the nil Value is specifically the cause. I independently re-confirmed at HEAD that loader.go:455 dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value. NOT verified: I did not enumerate every consumer's recover posture.

Suggested fix
-------------
Add if c.Value == nil { break } (fall through to the nil-safe drillIntoField) before touching c.Value.AdditionalProperties. One line.

Also cleared (stated, not claimed)
----------------------------------
The allOf/anyOf $ref diamond does not blow up: Schema.validate threads its stack through the return and never pops it, acting as a global pointer-keyed visited-set (executed N=10..30, microseconds). External-ref SSRF/path-traversal is blocked by default (IsExternalRefsAllowed=false); the known custom-ReadFromURIFunc bypass is the already-banked downstream oasdiff item.

Advisory-source note
--------------------
Five-source enumeration: every kin-openapi advisory (CVE-2025-30153 plus the five fresh July-2026 GHSAs) is in openapi3filter (request validation); this finding is in the openapi3 loader, untouched by that systematic reporter and flagged un-analyzed by the prior oasdiff scout. Not contested on the loader surface as of today (a systematic hunter could pivot, so it decays; submit reasonably promptly).

Dedup
-----
Dedup gate clean: no kin-openapi loader verdict in COVERED-INDEX, DISCLOSURE-INDEX or SCOUT-EXCLUDE (the one DISCLOSURE-INDEX hit is report #313, the downstream oasdiff, a different repo/lane).

Tooling
-------
AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with negative controls (a one-schema self-referential additionalProperties $ref crashes LoadFromData while a resolved additionalProperties and a normal recursive schema load fine), and I confirmed at HEAD that loader.go:455 dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value, on a load path with no recover.

## Summary
The `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler` (the exported, documented request-validation middleware) hard-wires the legacy router (`routers/legacy`). That router matches the incoming request method verbatim against a trie built exclusively from upper-cased canonical HTTP methods. A request carrying a method token that is not one of the 9 standard methods — a legitimate-but-unsupported token such as `PROPFIND`, or a non-canonical case variant such as lowercase `get` — misses the trie, leaves `route == nil`, and for an existing **static** path falls through to `PathItem.GetOperation(method)`, whose `default:` case calls `panic(...)`. The panic fires inside route resolution, **before any authentication** runs. This is an unauthenticated, remotely triggerable denial of service (recovered per-connection panic + unbounded error-log growth).

## Root Cause
- `openapi3filter/validation_handler.go:39` — `ValidationHandler.Load()` always constructs `legacyrouter.NewRouter(doc)`; there is no alternative router option on this path.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:109` — the request method is used verbatim (`method, url := req.Method, ...`); there is no canonicalization or rejection of unknown method tokens.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:69-70` — the trie is populated with `strings.ToUpper(method)` keys taken from `pathItem.Operations()` (canonical `http.Method*` constants only).
- `routers/legacy/router.go:141` — `root.Match(method + " " + remainingPath)` misses for a non-canonical/unsupported method → `route == nil`.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:146-150` — in the `route == nil` block, `doc.Paths.Value(path)` returns non-nil for an existing static path, and control reaches `pathItem.GetOperation(method)`.
- `openapi3/path_item.go:174` — `GetOperation`'s `switch method` has no matching case → `default: panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`.

## Impact
An unauthenticated attacker sends a single request with a non-standard HTTP method token to any existing static path. The handler goroutine panics; Go's `net/http` recovers the panic per connection (process survives), aborts the connection (client sees a reset / 500), and logs a full stack trace. Repeated requests cause connection churn and unbounded `http: panic serving` log growth, and the request never reaches authentication. Availability impact (A:L) under the default synchronous `ValidationHandler` middleware; on non-net/http hosts or when reached on an application goroutine the ceiling is a full crash.

## Proof of Concept
Serve any spec with a static path (e.g. `/ping`) behind `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler`, then:
```
printf 'PROPFIND /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n' | nc target 8080   # connection aborted (panic)
printf 'get /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n'      | nc target 8080   # connection aborted (panic)
printf 'GET /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n'      | nc target 8080   # 200 OK (process survived)
```

items.title: Gotify: Insufficiently Protected Password Change endpoint
items.summary:
The password change endpoint (`POST /current/user/password`) in Gotify versions <= 2.9.1 does not require knowledge of the current password. An attacker in possession of a valid client token can set a new password for the affected user. Recovering the account requires administrator intervention or direct database access.

## PoC

```bash
# Attacker has obtained a client token
# No prior password knowledge required
STOLEN_TOKEN="Cxxxxxxxxxx"

curl -X POST "http://gotify-host/current/user/password?token=${STOLEN_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"pass":"attacker_controls_this"}'
# Expected response:
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

## Mitigation

- Upgrade to Gotify 3.0.0, which introduces step-up authentication: changing the  password now requires re-authenticating with the account password, or
- Restrict access to the state-changing endpoints under `/user` and  `/current/user` to trusted networks.
